# Synthesis Principles {.unnumbered}

Part VII runs the subsystems of Parts I through VI together on one trajectory and asks which subsystem owns each transition when all of them act at once, and what work remains that no subsystem can take over. No single part could answer either question. The first returns to principles the reader already holds, from the invariant closure principle (\ref{pri-invariant-closure}) through the fleet principles of Part VI, and shows which subsystem closes which H·S·A exposure. The second has a single answer, and it is the volume's final principle.

::: {#pri-vol3-specification-boundary .callout-principle title="The specification boundary"}

**Invariant**: An agent can generate the realization of a design, such as code and configuration, but it cannot author the task contract that governs its own work, meaning the goal, the environment, the permitted actions, the available observations, and the completion criteria. If realization is a fraction $f$ of the engineering effort, accelerating it without limit bounds the net speedup at $1/(1-f)$.

**Implication**: Engineering effort shifts toward specifying invariants, building the verifiers that accept work, and owning the decision to accept. Faster generation raises the value of that work rather than removing it.

:::

The principle marks where the Stochastic Computer ends. The machine can close horizon, state, and authority for a task it has been given, and it can check its own work against a predicate that someone has written. Writing that predicate and answering for the result stay with the engineer. @Sec-vol3-conclusion traces one trajectory through every subsystem and ends on this boundary.
